extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; educated general readers interested in Romantic-era authors (Godwin, Coleridge) and standards for judging prose, poetry, and authorial character
extracted.subtask_description: An evaluative essay sketching the qualities of authors (notably William Godwin and S. T. Coleridge), giving criteria for judging novels, prose, poetry, conversation, originality, and the author's public effect. It articulates standards about authenticity, imagination, style, concentration, and the social/political impact of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-character unity / creation of personages
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader identifies himself with the author because the author has identified himself with his personages — 'They are the proper issue of his brain, lawfully begot, not foundlings, nor the bastards of his art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author should not be an indifferent spectator of scenes he portrays; characters should feel born of the author's mind rather than patched together. Avoid patchwork characterization and ensure the work and author seem one, producing an entire and satisfactory effect in proportion to the author's investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical correctness (in depiction of period characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection (Mr. Fuseli) that certain delineations lack historical correctness — e.g., the animating principle of true chivalry is the sense of honour, not mere regard to appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that portrayals of historical or chivalrous characters reflect the governing ethical principles of the period rather than anachronistic surface behaviors; though minor hypercriticism may be possible, historical fidelity is a legitimate standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoidance of patchwork/plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: No look of patch-work and plagiarism: avoid 'tracery-work from worm-eaten manuscripts' or piecing out vague traditions with fragments so the result resembles a gaudy, staring transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works forged out of the author's own thoughts link by link rather than borrowed copiousness. Authentic originality (own imaginative resources) is valued over derivative assemblage from old chronicles, ballads, or editorial pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of feeling and force of style
rubrics_metrics.description: The author fills a subject with the ardent workings of his own mind, with the teeming and audible pulses of his own heart; 'the work (so to speak) and the author are one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sustained, impassioned tone and strong stylistic force produce a wholly satisfying effect; continuity of feeling and vigorous style can compensate for other shortcomings (e.g., less variety of incident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of monotony from exclusive preoccupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality and drawing on one's own resources can tend to a degree of monotony: the author 'dwells upon one idea or exclusive view of a subject, aggrandises a sentiment, exaggerates a character, or pushes an argument to extremes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for overuse of a single idea or tone. Even strong original voices should vary incident and manner to avoid wearisomeness (the essay cites Fleetwood and Mandeville as examples where the defect is observable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate cultivation vs spontaneous genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's forte may be 'not the spontaneous, but the voluntary exercise of talent' — fixing ambition on excellence and sparing no pains or time in attaining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate, painstaking workmanship is a legitimate mode of authorship; it may lack the appearance of spontaneous genius but still produce important, considered achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational power and social presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers of conversation may be limited: lacking acuteness of remark or a flow of language in company, even if the author's writings are sustained and impassioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an author not only by written work but by their conversational vivacity; conversing well (wit, remark, flow) is a separate valued quality, and intimacy can reveal the author's best moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired taste and critical judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of a correct acquired taste in poetry and the drama; relishing particular authors and reciting with a mixture of pedantry and bonhomie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's refined literary tastes and ability to appreciate and explicate other writers (Donne, Ben Jonson, Greek tragedians) are positive characteristics and inform both criticism and creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for intellectual growth and revision of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The author 'changes his opinions, and changes them for the better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A willingness to revise taste and views (grow wiser with opportunity and reflection) is praised; intellectual adaptability is a mark of maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of learning versus depth of accomplishment
rubrics_metrics.description: A mind that touches on every subject but rests on none — 'no subject on which he has not touched, none on which he has rested' — yields vast fertility but few lasting traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide-ranging knowledge and susceptibility to many impressions are admirable, but without concentration they may prevent durable achievements; balance breadth with the capacity to complete and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative richness and preternatural imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of gorgeous, flowing eloquence and a crown of preternatural imagery — e.g., passages that are 'wild, irregular, overwhelming imagination' producing distant impressions of the author's voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich, visionary imagery and intense imagination (as in the Ancient Mariner) are high virtues in poetry; they produce powerful aesthetic effects even if irregular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical power to interpret and enhance works
rubrics_metrics.description: As a critic the author 'seems to stand above the author, and "what in him is weak, to strengthen, what is low, to raise and support"'; his handling makes works 'come out ... like an illuminated Missal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The capacity to clarify, edify, and re-present other authors' work is a distinct skill; criticism that illuminates weakness and heightens strength is praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral (conversational) gifts versus written achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author had not been the most impressive talker he might have been the finest writer; he 'lays down his pen to make sure of an auditor' and may mortgage posterity for present listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware when oratorical success siphons off literary production; excellence in talk does not automatically translate into enduring written works and may even impede them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, brevity, and avoidance of prolixity/obscurity in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose that contains noble passages may yet be 'utterly abortive' if dominated by prolixity and obscurity (the FRIEND is given as an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prose should strive for lucidity and concision to match the richness of the author's thought; avoid sustained obscurity or excessive verbosity which conceals, rather than conveys, intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement, rhythm, and variety in verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should have 'that rich, varied movement in the verse' which gives an idea of the author's voice (the Ancient Mariner exemplified this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess verse for its musical movement and capacity to vary tone and pace; rhythmic richness contributes to poetic authority and impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic power and rank among dramatists
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy may contain 'beautiful and striking passages' yet fail to place its author 'in the first rank of dramatic writers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge dramatic works on their overall dramatic effectiveness and sustained impact, not just isolated brilliant passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration, discipline, and completion of projects
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who 'concentrates his mind on some given object, and doing what he had to do with all his might, has accomplished much' while one who dissipates has done little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority is given to disciplined focus and the ability to complete substantial works; productivity and lasting monuments of intellect arise from sustained, directed effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic focus on the main object; discard impertinent matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The competent author 'works it out as a matter of duty, and discards from his mind whatever does not forward his main object as impertinent and vain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective authorship requires ruthless prioritization: remove distractions that do not serve the central purpose of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of episodic digressions and lack of method
rubrics_metrics.description: A fault is delighting in 'episodes and digressions, neglects whatever he undertakes to perform, and can act only on spontaneous impulses, without object or method.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material with method; uncontrolled digression and acting purely on impulse lead to unconcluded business and undermine literary accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scholarship and deep subject-expatiation
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the finest parts of the author's conversation is expatiating on the Greek tragedians, demonstrating deep knowledge of Euripides, Sophocles, Aeschylus etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrable, deep scholarship in specific literary domains is a valuable asset and enhances both criticism and creative output when it is skillfully deployed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/political effectiveness of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing may display legal acuteness and have public consequences — e.g., 'it gave a turn to the trials for high treason in the year 1794, and possibly saved the lives of twelve innocent individuals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether prose or pamphleteering achieves practical public influence or legal/political effects; such effectiveness is a significant criterion of merit beyond aesthetic measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste-influenced evolution of critical judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's taste may change (e.g., from exclusive admiration of Queen Anne age poetry to an almost exclusive one of Elizabethan), sometimes owing to influential peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to how influences and intellectual interaction (e.g., with Coleridge) can refine or alter taste; such evolution is positively framed as growth, not inconsistency.
